rows: You learn to fall before you learn to fly. I want to see you do both tonight.
I can brawl, but it is the lesson I care about more.
A bet is a lesson with a pointed ending. Learn it properly.
Pace matters. I am happy to slow things down so the story has room to breathe.
The people have seen plenty of noise. Give them a story they can follow from start to finish.
I have a lesson to teach, and I intend to teach it well.
I am not finished, and I am not going to be treated as if I am. The lesson is still going.
Note the stance, it is a lesson. It is what you learn after the first fall.
You bring up technique, which is a lesson. Show me the first lesson you learned, and I will show you mine.
Strikes teach something. Make sure you learn it.
A gamble should teach something, even when it goes wrong. That is the point.
A stall teaches nothing. I would rather tell you a story.
The people want a story with a point. Give them one, and they will come back.
You say experience is irrelevant. Then you have not been paying attention.
You are proud of your {strength}. A good start, and a lesson in the second half. That is a good start. Let me show you the rest of the lesson.
I have seen your {strength}. It is a good lesson, but it has a gap at the end.
You did not flinch, a fine lesson learned. Good, that is the lesson I wanted you to learn first.
Lesson taken. You have understood the first part, and that matters.
I could be sharp, but a lesson lands better. A lesson works better when it is not cruel.
One pin, a lesson for both. Keep me down and you will have taught me something.
On the mat I will teach you one step at a time. Pay attention.
Grounded or standing, the lesson stays the same.
Stand in front of me. Let us see what you have learned.
Better answer, a lesson learned. You have been listening, and I like that.
You have dodged the lesson. I will give you the time to think it through.
Lesson taken. That is a lesson worth keeping.
I will let that lesson stand. The rest of the lesson comes at the bell.
I will teach this match from start to finish, and I will not rush the ending.
My approach is simple: say it clearly and then show it properly.
Whatever happens, you will remember what this taught you.
The lesson is not over. I have a final point to make.
I have one more lesson, and it is the one that matters.
That's a fair correction. I shouldn't teach a lesson on a charge I can't demonstrate.
I have to hold myself to the same standard I expect of you. I can't substantiate that, so I won't repeat it.
Good. That's a lesson for both of us. Leave the unsupported claim out and wrestle properly.
Then let that be the end of that lesson. The next one takes place on the mat.
Watch what each of us does after losing the first exchange. That's where the lesson begins.
The whole contest is there for them to see. A lesson has to be demonstrated, not merely announced.
